text: Everything in this chapter so far connected whole networks -- site-to-site VPN links an entire on-prem office to a VNet or VPC, and ExpressRoute or Direct Connect do the same over a dedicated circuit. Point-to-site VPN connects a single device, one laptop, directly into a VNet or VPC, with no on-prem VPN device needed at the user's location at all -- just a client application and valid credentials.

In Azure, a user installs the Azure VPN Client, or configures a built-in OS client using a protocol Azure supports, and authenticates either with a certificate issued to their device or through Microsoft Entra ID sign-in, depending on how the gateway is configured. AWS's equivalent is AWS Client VPN, an endpoint the user's OpenVPN-based client connects to, authenticated via certificates, Active Directory, or federated SSO.

Once connected, the laptop behaves, for that session, as if it had a private IP address inside the cloud network -- able to reach private resources that were never exposed to the public internet, like an internal database or an admin console with no public endpoint. The rest of the laptop's traffic can still go straight to the regular internet, depending on how the VPN client is configured.

That's the specific problem point-to-site solves: a remote employee needing direct access to private cloud resources without first connecting through a full office VPN or physically being on the corporate network. The old workaround routed everything through a site-to-site VPN back to the office, then out to the cloud from there -- extra latency, extra infrastructure, and a dependency on the office network staying up. Point-to-site skips that chain entirely; the laptop talks to the cloud gateway directly.

That closes out private connectivity for this course -- site-to-site VPN, dedicated circuits, and now point-to-site, each solving a different shape of connection problem. Chapter 7 turns to compliance in the cloud, starting with the shared responsibility model revisited specifically through that lens.
